name: Spray-in temporary hair color

lead: Spray-in temporary hair color is a wash-out pigment sprayed onto dry hair. Wikipedia lists sprays among the forms of temporary color, alongside rinses, shampoos, gels and foams, and says temporary color is typically brighter and more vibrant than semi-permanent or permanent color.

It is most often used for occasions such as Christmas and Halloween costume parties. Some people also use tinted sprays to blend gray roots or darken thinning areas for the day, since the color needs no commitment and comes out at the next wash.

paras: The product is sprayed onto dry hair in sections, left to dry and styled, and removed with shampoo. Because the pigment sits on the surface, it can transfer to clothing, pillows and skin when it is not fully dry.

Wikipedia notes that color particles stay on the hair surface and are easily removed with one shampoo, though color can persist on very dry or damaged hair. Hair dye products can stain skin at the hairline, and some recommend a patch test before use, though European dermatologists have advised against pre-use testing because it can add sensitization risk.

lead: Spray-in temporary hair color is a wash-out hair dye applied from an aerosol or spray. It belongs to the temporary category of hair color, whose forms Wikipedia lists as rinses, shampoos, gels, sprays and foams.[1] The color is typically brighter and more vibrant than semi-permanent or permanent dyes and is most often used for occasions such as Christmas and Halloween costume parties.[1]

People use it to change how their hair looks for a single event or day: bold costume colors, temporary highlights, or tinted coverage of gray roots and thin patches. Because the product does not alter the hair's interior and rinses out, it carries no long-term change in appearance.

According to Wikipedia, temporary pigments cannot penetrate the cuticle layer; the color particles remain attached to the surface of the hair shaft and can be removed with a single shampoo, though temporary color can persist on very dry or damaged hair into which the pigment can migrate.[1]
infobox: Pigment stays on the hair surface and does not enter the cuticle [1]
Costume parties; temporary coverage of grays or thin areas [1]

paras: Wikipedia explains that temporary hair color pigments are too large to pass through the cuticle, so they sit on the surface of the strand rather than changing the hair from within.[1] This is why the result fades with washing and why the shade shows up strongly on light hair and less on dark hair.

Wikipedia's general hair coloring article says drips and slips can discolor skin, especially with darker shades and dry skin, and that the discoloration typically fades in a few days to a week as the skin renews. It also notes that many hair color products recommend a patch test 48 hours before use, while European dermatologists have advised against pre-use testing because it can add sensitization risk and lay people may misread results.[1] The article does not give safety information specific to sprays.
